History & Physical (Super Detailed)

Consult Summary:
• 33-year-old woman presents via tele-visit with a 4-hour history of sudden, moderate-to-severe left-sided headache with visual “zig-zag” disturbance, nausea, and vomiting—clinical picture most consistent with first-episode migraine with aura; safety-net given to exclude secondary causes.

History:
• Presenting complaint – “really strong” left-sided headache started abruptly this morning.
  – Onset: Sudden, first episode of this kind, ~4 hours before consult.
  – Location: Left side; sometimes feels “behind the eye.”
  – Severity: Rates 6/10 (kidney-stone pain previously =10/10).
  – Character/progression: Constant since onset; worsens with head movement; prefers to keep head still.
  – Associated symptoms:
      • Blurred vision with zig-zag lines (visual aura).
      • Dizziness.
      • Photophobia – “cannot stand screens.”
      • Nausea with two episodes of vomiting at onset; nausea persists.
      • No limb weakness, speech difficulty, gait disturbance, or other focal neurologic deficit.
  – Exacerbating factors: Moving, leaving bed.
  – Relieving factors tried: Paracetamol taken ~3 h ago—no benefit.
• Review of systems (limited to information provided):
  – Neurologic: No weakness, no sensory loss, no ataxia.
  – General: No fever reported.
  – ENT/neck: No neck pain or stiffness reported.
  – Cardiopulmonary, GI (other than nausea/vomiting), GU: Not discussed.
• Patient concerns: Fears brain tumour or stroke; wonders if she should go to Emergency Department.

Past Medical History:
• Kidney stones (dates/details not specified).
• No prior history of migraine.
• No other chronic illnesses noted.

Medications:
• None routinely.
• Paracetamol today – dose/route/frequency not documented.

Allergies:
• Denies known drug allergies.

Social History:
• Pregnancy considered “really doubt it” by patient.
• Smoking, alcohol, drug use, occupation, and living situation not discussed.

Family History:
• Mother – migraines.
• Mother – hypothyroidism.
• No other relevant family illnesses mentioned.

Physical Examination:
(Tele-visit; no hands-on exam performed)
• Vitals: Not obtained.
• General appearance (per discussion): Alert, conversational.
• Neurologic (history-based): No self-reported focal deficits; ambulates normally.
• No additional exam findings documented.

Investigations:
• None to date.

Assessment & Plan:
Issue 1 – Acute unilateral headache, likely migraine with aura
  • Assessment: Fits classic migraine features (unilateral pain, visual aura, nausea/vomiting, photophobia, family history). First presentation at age 33 still plausible.
  • Plan:
      – Start simple regimen: Ibuprofen (dose/route not documented) plus over-the-counter anti-emetic; drink sugary carbonated beverage (e.g., Coca-Cola) as advised.
      – Provide written migraine advice sheet (pharmacy-level options, trigger avoidance).
      – Schedule same-day in-person appointment for full neurologic examination; patient may cancel if symptoms fully resolve.
      – Educate on expected course: attacks may last 4–72 h; seek help if no improvement within ~40 min after meds.

Issue 2 – Exclude serious secondary headache (e.g., subarachnoid hemorrhage, arterial dissection)
  • Assessment: Sudden onset “first” headache warrants caution; current pain only 6/10, no neuro deficits, lowers but does not eliminate risk.
  • Plan:
      – Safety-net advice: Go to Emergency Department or call emergency services if headache becomes the “worst ever,” any neck stiffness, confusion, weakness, visual loss, collapse, or persistent vomiting.
      – Reiterate availability of urgent clinic review if condition deteriorates before scheduled visit.

Issue 3 – Patient anxiety/hypochondriasis
  • Assessment: Expressed significant worry about catastrophic causes.
  • Plan:
      – Provide reassurance regarding likely migraine diagnosis and outlined red-flag signs.
      – Offer follow-up for further discussion of anxiety if needed.

Summary of Differential Diagnoses (from DDx):
1. Migraine with aura – High likelihood. Classic unilateral headache, visual aura, nausea/vomiting, photophobia, family history; no focal deficits.
2. Subarachnoid hemorrhage – Moderate likelihood. Sudden onset “first” headache with vomiting; mitigated by moderate pain score and lack of neurological signs.
3. Carotid/vertebral artery dissection – Low–moderate likelihood. Unilateral headache with visual disturbance and dizziness; no neck pain/trauma or neuro deficit.

Quality checks:
● Missing but expected: Vital signs, complete systems review, full medication/allergy reconciliation, detailed social history (smoking/alcohol/drugs), obstetric/gynecologic history.  
● Conflicts: None noted between transcript and DDx.  
● Transcript quality: Clear overall; minor connection interruptions but clinical content preserved.
